title: ‘You’re protecting Trump’: Hanson-Young clashes with Liberal senator before digital duty of care legislation passes – as it happened
description:

Wells says AI investment and creative protections not a ‘zero-sum game’

Weighing into the gigantic debate that is AI companies wanting to scrape Australian data to train models versus creatives who want to protect their work, Anika Wells says it’s not a ‘zero-sum’ game.

I reject this sort of zero-sum game where building Australian sovereignty in AI must come at the expense of creatives or at diminishing the rights of creatives. At the moment, yes, we want deals, but we want creatives paid properly for their work. And the situation that we find ourselves in at the moment is that they’re not. They have no control and often no payment for their work.
text: What we learnt today, Wednesday 25 November
That’s where we’ll leave things for today. Thanks for reading, as always. Here were our top stories:

Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data was released showing inflation surged to 4.9% in the year to October, from 4.3% in the 12 months to September, amid fears Australia could tip into recession next year.
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, said it was a “very serious moment” for our economy and the government would have to make “difficult decisions” to try to curb the rising cost of living.

Former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon was found guilty of murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies with his service weapon. A New South Wales supreme court jury delivered its verdict after two hours of deliberation on Wednesday, finding Lamarre-Condon guilty of two counts of murder.
The NSW government said it was scaling up its fire ant response after confirming a nest detected in the state was “larger and more complex” than initially thought.
A coronial inquest into the deaths of babies in or after freebirths in northern NSW heard evidence from birth keeper Sita Kali, who said she doubted her psychic abilities after two babies died.
About 100 football clubs, representing hundreds of thousands of players, deliberately missed the deadline to sign up for next season amid a dispute with Football Queensland over $5 gate fees.
And Matildas keeper Teagan Micah revealed head trauma-induced neurological disorder almost ended career.
Digital duty of care bill to become law after passing federal parliament
Following that exchange, the digital duty of care bill has now passed both houses of parliament. The Coalition tried a last-minute procedural tactic to delay its passage, but it was not successful.
The bill passed the lower house 97 votes to 43. Labor, Greens and some of the teal crossbenchers voted in favour, while the Coalition, Dai Le, Bob Katter and One Nation voted against it.

Following the bill’s passage, Angus Taylor attempted to move a suspension of standing orders to debate a motion, calling for the government to be censured “for its dirty deal with the Greens political party to ram through this parliament its Digital Duty of Care Bill, which will censor political opinion, restrict freedom of speech and ultimately fail to protect Australian families”.
The motion was unsuccessful.
‘You and Trump can line up’: Hanson-Young’s dig at Henderson

Labor’s digital duty of care legislation spurred a verbal spar between Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young and Coalition shadow minister Sarah Henderson in the halls of the press gallery a short time ago.

The legislation was about to pass with the Greens’ support. Henderson was about to hold a doorstop interview to criticise the bill and pledge the Coalition would repeal it when Hanson-Young walked past on her way to a TV interview.
As Hanson-Young edged past, Henderson joked: “Do you want to join me help repeal the digital duty of care?”
Hanson-Young, whose negotiations with Labor led to significant strengthening of the bill, replied: “Not ever.”
Henderson laughed, but Hanson-Young continued: “You and Trump can line up, Sarah, if you want.”
Henderson: “Good on you Sarah. Never miss an opportunity ... we’re protecting the free speech of Australians.”
Hanson-Young shot back: “You’re protecting Trump.”
Icac finds female NSW prison staff faced ‘boys club’ culture and harassment
A NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) inquiry has found female prison staff who faced boys club-style harassment and abuse were failed by managers, AAP reports.

Investigators uncovered a “boys club” culture which “tolerated harassment and abuse of mainly female colleagues”. Icac investigated grave misconduct allegations, including claims of disrespectful language, sexual assaults, and reprisals for reporting offensive behaviour.
The commission said that culture discouraged employees from making complaints. But it did not find Corrective Services NSW to be corrupt.
Corrective Services NSW accepted the findings and recommendations and was developing an action plan, a spokesperson said.
Conversion ‘therapy’ survivor welcomes new laws in Tasmania outlawing practice
Glen Worrell, who went through two decades of conversion practices aimed at changing his sexual orientation, hopes new laws in Tasmania mean others will never have to do the same, AAP reports.
The island state’s upper house of parliament today passed legislation to ban the practice, giving the green light for the changes to become law.
Conversion practices, often labelled as a “therapy”, are aimed at changing or suppressing someone’s sexual orientation or gender identity.
The reforms in Tasmania come after a decade-long campaign and bring the state into line with NSW, Victoria, Queensland, South Australia and the ACT. Worrell said:

double quotation markI was quite elated and relieved. I did wonder if we would reach this moment at times. I wasn’t sure if there would be amendments that would disempower the bill. But I think it’s strong. I believe it will save lives.
The laws include several nation-leading features such as the creation of a commissioner to educate, prevent and respond to any conversion practices.
Survivors can receive financial compensation and there is a mandatory responsibility for government bodies to refer conversion practices to the commissioner.
The laws make it a criminal offence if people intentionally engage in conversion practices or they cause injury, as well as if negligence towards injury is evident.

The passage of the Tasmanian laws comes on the same day that the federal government issued a formal apology to current and former serving members of the Australian Defence Force for harm experienced as a result of discriminatory policies based on individuals’ sexual orientation.
‘We still have a number of things going for us’, treasurer says as he denies Australia in ‘stagflation’
Jim Chalmers has denied Australia is experiencing “stagflation” after the release of grim inflation data today, saying “we still have a number of things going for us”.
At a broad level, stagflation refers to persistent levels of inflation with moderate to poor (in other words, stagnant) economic growth, and elevated unemployment.

During his ABC Afternoon Briefing today, it was put to Chalmers that, given Australia was experiencing rising unemployment, inflation, and interest rates, that was “kind of the recipe for stagflation”. Chalmers replied:

double quotation markThe reason why that term doesn’t fit our situation is because we still have a labour market, which is, by historical standards, pretty robust. We’ve got growth, which is faster than any major advanced economy except for the US. We’ve got wages growth above 3%. And so, even in the context of this combination of challenges and risks and uncertainties and pressures, which are in our economy – and we acknowledge that – we still have a number of things going for us as well, and that is why that description doesn’t quite fit us.
Treasurer promises government savings to help in fight against inflation
The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, says the government will have to make “difficult decisions” to respond to the surging cost of living after the release of new inflation data today.

Inflation surged to 4.9% in the year to October, from 4.3% in the 12 months to September, Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) data released earlier today showed, amid fears Australia could tip into recession next year.

Although the ABS said the “temporary shocks” of surging fuel costs and the end of electricity rebates drove the larger-than-expected lift in consumer prices, the Coalition has claimed government spending by Labor is fuelling inflation.
Speaking on the ABC’s Afternoon Briefing program a short time ago, Chalmers said inflation was increasing in every major advanced economy, and that the government took its responsibilities seriously.

Chalmers has been preparing to present a mid-year budget update in three weeks’ time, which he called a “mini budget”, and said the government had a three-part plan to deal with the cost of living crunch. He said:

double quotation markThere will be a number of new savings and that’s because we take our responsibilities very seriously in the fight against inflation. Three parts of our plan, first of all in relation to inflation, running a tight ship in the budget, providing some cost-of-living relief but making it as responsible as possible Obviously there are issues around how hard it is for first home buyers to crack the market, and so our tax reforms are primarily about that. And thirdly, [the] speed limit on our economy is too slow … We have to lift [the] growth agenda – cutting compliance costs, speeding up approvals.
You can read more about the jump in inflation in this story by our economics editor, Patrick Commins:
Australia to provide Solomon Islands with $740m under landmark agreement
Australia will provide Solomon Islands $740m over the decade as part of its landmark treaty with the Pacific nation.
Under the agreement, Honiara will not allow its territory to be used for a foreign military base. Developmental assistance will be provided through $670m in grants and $70m in loans.
Australia will help bridge the funding gap for Solomon Islands prime minister Matthew Wale’s national free education policy, a key pledge of his government.
About a third of children in the Solomon Islands don’t go to school due to costs, and only 19% complete year 12.
Money is expected to start flowing to Honiara in January, when Solomon Islands’ parliament returns.

Australia is racing to ensure ordinary people feel the benefits of the deal as soon as possible before expected Chinese-backed attempts to scupper the treaty get under way. The Solomon Islands is expected to face backlash from Beijing over the agreement, as Honiara chooses not to renew its five-year security pact with China when it expires next April.
The treaty with Australia also contains climate commitments.
Funding should be diverted if Closing the Gap principles breached, commissioner says

Australia’s commissioner for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and young people says federal funding for child protection should be diverted from state and territory governments that breach the principles of the National Agreement on Closing the Gap.

At the National Press Club earlier today, commissioner Sue-Anne Hunter outlined concerns of a child protection system “going backwards” in Australia, and said the governments needed to be accountable for “failing systems”.

It comes after the federal minister for Indigenous Australians, Malarndirri McCarthy, withheld about $80m from then Northern Territory Remote Area Investment (NTRAI) between the commonwealth and NT, before the closure of Darwin’s largest Aboriginal homeless shelter.

double quotation mark[Diverting funding] is a step forward about accountability and it should go to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander organisations, to be able to do the work that’s needed. What I’m finding is when I look at these frameworks and everything that’s decided, is that no one is actually held accountable. People are more likely to walk through the door of an Aboriginal community-controlled organisation than […] of a mainstream one and get the help that’s required.
Hello, thanks for reading so far. I’ll take you through the rest of the news this afternoon.
Thank you all for following along on the blog – and what a day it has been!
I’ll leave you with the lovely Catie McLeod for the rest of the afternoon and see you here bright and early tomorrow.
Tl;dr here’s what happened in question time
The prime minister and Jim Chalmers copped plenty of heat, urged to take responsibility for the less less-than-ideal inflation numbers today.
The treasurer hit back, arguing that it “took some nerve” for the Coalition to attack him considering its economic record.
Dan Tehan called Tony Burke a “dibber-dobber” after he said Angus Taylor interjected 17 times in one question, including “three non-verbal grunts”.
Independent MP Nicolette Boele said the government lacked credibility at Cop because it keeps expanding fossil fuel projects.
And two Nationals – Pat Conaghan and Darren Chester – were booted from the chamber for being too loud.
What do Labor and the French Revolution have in common?
They both love a guillotine.

Labor, with the support of the Greens, have passed a motion in the Senate that will “guillotine” debate (i.e cut it short) and expedite a vote on five bills including the private health insurance bill and trusts tax bill.
It means they’ll be debated and voted on by 7:30pm tonight.
Those bills that pass with amendments in the Senate tonight will then go back to the House tomorrow.
‘A tragedy in the life of our nation’: prime minister apologises to LGBTQ+ veterans
Following the deputy prime minister’s national apology to LGBTQ+ veterans and service men and women, Anthony Albanese has also addressed the Parliament.
He says Australia’s national apology follows those in other nations.

He says the ban on homosexual soldiers from joining or staying in the Australian Defence Force until the 1990s was a “tragedy of the life of our nation, a callous chapter in which so many Australians who had selflessly chosen to serve their nation with pride had their courage repaid with inhumanity”:

double quotation markAn apology is never the end of the story. Nor can it have raised the damage already done, but it does open a new chapter. We thank everyone who made it possible. We mourn everyone who is no longer here to turn the page. Every one of you belongs in the Australian Defence Force. You should never have been made to feel otherwise.
The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, also acknowledges the suffering and hurt faced by those discriminated against and banned from the army.
double quotation markFor decades, ADF policy was wrong. ADF members suffered, veterans suffered, their families suffered, and none of them should have suffered.
Question time (finally) ends
After a final dixer to Daniel Mulino, the prime minister calls time on QT.
Boele pushes Labor on disaster preparedness ahead of summer
You might have noticed question time is going quite long today … believe me, so have I.
Nicolette Boele gets a second question and asks the emergency management what preparations are being made ahead of an El Niño summer. Kristy McBain, the minister for emergency management, says:

double quotation markThere are more than 520 disaster ready fund projects now happening across the country, through rounds one to four. Including with project partner contributions, $1.4bn in money going to risk reduction mitigation and resilience projects across the country. Our government has invested really heavily in emergency management.
